title: Byung-Chul Han
summary: Byung-Chul Han is a Korean-born philosopher who writes in German, the author of short books about how we live today. His central idea: what weighs on people now is no longer an external prohibition but an inner “you can” — an endless demand to be productive, successful and positive. Hence burnout, depression and the feeling that there is no more time and no more silence.
onEmotions: For Han, many heavy feelings are not only a personal story but also a symptom of an era he calls the “achievement society.” In such a society a person becomes an “entrepreneur of the self” and exploits themselves, and any difficult feeling is treated as an obstacle to efficiency. Han defends the right to negativity: to pain, pause, slowness, to meeting an Other who is truly unlike us. He proposes not to “optimize” feelings but to give them back time and space — through contemplative idleness, ritual, attention to the earth and to another person.

anxiety.text: “You can” is, for Han, our century's most demanding command, because it doesn't sound like one. Hence your anxiety, heavy and real: it is born less of outside threat than of too many possibilities. In the “achievement society” there is no strict overseer above us; instead, an endless “you can” sounds within: you can do more, better, faster. If everything is possible, then any failure seems to be only your fault — and anxiety becomes the background of life. Han calls this the “violence of positivity”: pressure that comes not from prohibition but from endless encouragement. Seeing it this way lifts part of the burden. Your anxiety is not proof that you are doing something wrong; it is a natural response to a world with no point of “enough.” You can let yourself see that some of these demands come not from you but from the era.
anxiety.practice: Say your main “I must” for today under your breath, then say it again, this time starting with “The achievement society wants me to…”. Listen to which version sounds more honest.

fear.text: Picture a corridor that narrows with every step: that, for Han, is what fear does to the world. Your fear is honest all the same — it tells you that something matters to you and could be lost. In his late book The Spirit of Hope, Han describes our time as an age saturated with fear: fear of not keeping up, of falling behind, of dropping out of the race, of becoming unneeded. But Han does not ask us to be ashamed of fear. He sets hope against it — not naive optimism, but openness to what has not yet happened. Taking Han's thought further, your fear does not have to be defeated by willpower. It is enough to notice that it is not the whole world, and to leave a small window for the possible beside it. Fear and hope can coexist.
fear.practice: Place a palm on your chest and take three slow breaths, and on each out-breath say to yourself: “And yet it is possible…”. For Han, hope begins with just such a tiny crack in the wall of fear.

sadness.text: A life without pain, for Han, is a life without touch: smooth, convenient and flat. Your sadness needs no permission, even when everyone around you is expected to “stay positive.” Han criticizes what he calls the “palliative society”: a contemporary culture that fears any pain and rushes to numb it right away — with entertainment, a like, a pill, a motivational quote. He calls this fear of pain “algophobia.” For Han, pain and sorrow are a contact with reality, with what does not bend to our will. This view lets you treat sadness not as a breakdown to be fixed urgently but as a form of depth. Sadness slows you down, and in that slowing, what Han values most can appear — attention to the world and to yourself.
sadness.practice: Rest your palm where the sadness sits in your body and breathe under it for a minute, without picking up a screen. Let it be a touch, not a treatment.

grief.text: Our time has almost no form for farewell — no clothing, no words, no set period — and Han sees this as one of the quiet troubles of the age. Your grief is the price of having loved, and it does not have to pass “on schedule.” In The Disappearance of Rituals Han describes rituals as what makes time habitable, the way a house makes space habitable. Mourning was once exactly such a ritual — long, shared, with the right not to hurry anywhere. Han would probably say: if it seems to you that your grief has “dragged on,” perhaps the problem is not you but a culture that demands you get back in line quickly. Your grief deserves time, form and witnesses.
grief.practice: Choose one gesture of remembrance and repeat it three times, slowly, like a rite: light a candle, set a cup on the table, say the name aloud. Ritual, for Han, holds time when it is hard to hold it yourself.

loneliness.text: The screen you look into, for Han, mostly works as a mirror: it hands you back yourself. Hence this ache — a living need for a person who will not be your reflection. Han notices a paradox: we have never been so “connected” and never suffered so much from loneliness. In The Agony of Eros he describes the “hell of the same”: the digital world mostly shows us reflections of ourselves — similar opinions, similar tastes. The Other disappears — the one who is truly different and can surprise us. Connections multiply while relationships grow thin. This view can bring relief: your loneliness is not proof that something is wrong with you. It is partly produced by the way the time we live in is arranged. And it points a direction — not toward more contacts, but toward one real encounter.
loneliness.practice: Ask someone a question today whose answer you can't guess in advance, and listen to the end without interrupting. That is the small encounter with the Other that Han writes about.

anger.text: What did the last storm of online outrage you saw actually change? Han would ask this to tell real anger apart from noise. Your anger says that something important has been touched — and so it deserves more than noise. In the book In the Swarm he distinguishes genuine anger from digital outrage — waves of indignation online that flare up quickly and die down just as quickly, changing nothing. Real anger, for Han, can interrupt the usual course of things and open up something new; it requires focus and time. Outrage, by contrast, is scattered and quickly runs out of breath. The simple conclusion: your anger needs neither to be suppressed nor to be vented immediately. It is worth hearing it and letting it ripen — then it can turn from a flash into a clear understanding of what is unacceptable to you and what you want to change.
anger.practice: Before you answer, let the anger ripen: put the reply off until tomorrow, and for now walk for five minutes carrying it with you like a heavy bag, noticing what it is protecting.

shame.text: Imagine a house with glass walls where every room is on view. That, in essence, is the world Han describes — and no wonder it is so easy to feel ashamed in it. Han writes about the “transparency society”: today everything must be exhibited, shown, rated. We constantly see ourselves through the eyes of others — through feeds, ratings, comparisons. The power he describes in Psychopolitics does not forbid; it urges us to lay ourselves open. In such a world shame easily becomes chronic: there will always be someone more beautiful, more successful, more productive. Han might add: part of your shame is an effect of constant exposure, not the truth about you. Han defends the right to opacity, to an inner space shown to no one. You have the right not to be fully visible — and in that shelter shame can quiet down.
shame.practice: Do one thing today just for yourself and tell no one about it — not online, not in conversation. Let yourself have a small room without glass.

guilt.text: In German, Schuld means both guilt and debt, and Han, following Walter Benjamin, sees capitalism as a religion that never forgives debts. If guilt won't let go, it is worth asking where it comes from. In the “achievement society” a person becomes an “entrepreneur of the self”: their own boss and their own worker. They exploit themselves voluntarily — and so they experience any failure as personal guilt rather than as a consequence of circumstances. Han writes that in this situation the exploiter and the exploited coincide. This view does not cancel real responsibility, but it separates it from endless self-accusation. You can ask yourself: did I really act badly — or am I simply failing to meet an impossible standard? In the second case guilt is not the voice of conscience but the voice of the era.
guilt.practice: Name aloud, in one sentence, the specific act you regret. If no such sentence comes and all that is left is “I'm not enough…”, that is not guilt but a debt to the era — and today you may leave it unpaid.

quote.text: The exploiter is simultaneously the exploited. Perpetrator and victim can no longer be distinguished.
quote.author: Byung-Chul Han

envy.text: Each of us today is a project to be endlessly improved, Han says, and other people's shop windows are always at hand for comparison. No wonder envy comes — an unpleasant but deeply human feeling, and admitting to it is already honest. We see the polished fragments of other people's lives and compare them with the underside of our own. Han calls this culture “positive”: it has no room for failure, boredom, ordinariness — only successes. Here is what follows: envy is not a flaw in your character but a predictable effect of a world where everything is put up for comparison. You can accept it as a signal: it points to what you really want — and at the same time to how little we know about other people's lives.
envy.practice: Imagine you got what you envy, but no one would ever know. Is the desire still there? Han would say: what remains is yours, and the rest is the shop window.

emptiness.text: Han's Narcissus is not a vain beauty but a person drowning in himself, because nothing truly other is left around him. The emptiness you feel is hard to explain, but it is real and deserves attention. Han considers depression and apathy characteristic states of our era. In his view, they arise not from lack but from excess: too many stimuli, goals, possibilities — and too little genuine connection with the Other and with the world. A person constantly busy optimizing themselves ends up closed in on themselves, and the world stops responding. This view can help: emptiness is not a verdict on who you are. Perhaps it is saying that what you lack is not new tasks but something external and real that you can simply contemplate.
emptiness.practice: Choose one thing that doesn't belong to you and wants nothing from you — a tree, a cloud, the wall of the house next door — and look at it for three minutes, until it becomes a little more real than your thoughts.

confusion.text: To extend Han's thought, information is like sand: plentiful, but you can't build a house from it. It is easy to feel lost in a world changing faster than we can make sense of it. Han writes a great deal about information overload: there is more and more information and less and less understanding. Information, he says, is fragmented and momentary, while knowledge and experience require time, coherence, narrative. In The Crisis of Narration he observes that we have forgotten how to tell the stories that give life meaning and direction. In other words, your confusion is not a sign of inability but a reasonable response to a flow that has no form. Instead of looking for even more information, you can slow down and try to put what you already know into a story of your own — even an unfinished one.
confusion.practice: Tell someone — or yourself, out loud — what is happening to you as a fairy tale: “Once upon a time there was a person who…”. Three or four sentences, no moral at the end.

fatigue.text: Prometheus chained to the rock is, for Han, not a hero but the first burnout: the eagle that pecks at his liver every day is his own “I must.” Your tiredness is real, and it is neither laziness nor personal failure. In The Burnout Society Han writes that the old disciplinary society rested on prohibitions, while today's “achievement society” rests on a freedom that turns into compulsion: we drive ourselves forward. The result is burnout: a person is exhausted because they endlessly compete with themselves. Han distinguishes a tiredness that isolates from another kind — the one Peter Handke wrote about: a tiredness that lets you let go, stop, and see the world again. This view gives permission: rest is not a reward for achievement but a necessary condition of life. Your tiredness can become not an end but a door to a slower existence.
fatigue.practice: Sit down and allow yourself the tiredness Handke wrote about: not fighting it but looking through it at the world — at the light in the room, at the street outside. Three minutes, with no goal of “recovering for work.”

quote.text: The disciplinary society produces madmen and criminals. Achievement society, in contrast, creates depressives and losers.
quote.author: Byung-Chul Han

boredom.text: “The dream bird that hatches the egg of experience” — that is what Walter Benjamin called boredom, and Han is fond of the line. So what looks like a waste of time is, for him, valuable. He writes with regret that we have forgotten how to be deeply bored: at the slightest pause we reach for a screen, switch, look for a stimulus. He calls this kind of attention “hyperattention” — scattered, jumping, unable to linger. And yet it is precisely deep boredom, for Han, that is the soil of creativity and contemplation. In this light your boredom is not a problem demanding an immediate solution but an opportunity. If you don't run from it right away, something new may emerge behind it: a thought, a wish, an image that would not have appeared amid constant busyness.
boredom.practice: Sit for three minutes somewhere nothing is happening — by a wall, at a bus stop, on the stairs — and don't take out your phone. Notice the moment when boredom stops being empty and something stirs in it.

quote.text: Boredom is the dream bird that hatches the egg of experience.
quote.author: Walter Benjamin
quote.source: “The Storyteller” (Han quotes these words in The Burnout Society)

joy.text: A festival, Han writes, is time that serves nothing — and that is exactly why it shines. Your joy needs no justification. Han suggests distinguishing joy from what he calls the cult of positivity. Constant cheerfulness, a “good mood” as a duty, the “like” as a unit of happiness — for him all this is not joy but one more form of pressure. Genuine joy, in his view, is closer to festivity and play: to states that serve nothing, produce nothing and are not built into the logic of usefulness. This view lets you simply be in your joy without turning it into content or into proof of success. Joy doesn't have to be recorded, displayed or justified — it is enough to live it.
joy.practice: Give this joy a tiny festival with no witnesses: open the window, stretch, walk slowly across the room — filming nothing and sending nothing to anyone.

love.text: In English you “fall” in love; Han would probably say that our culture wants love without the fall. The tenderness you feel is a sign that you are still able to fall. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that love is in danger today because it demands what the achievement society avoids: risk, vulnerability, an encounter with a truly Other. Eros, for Han, is a relation to someone who cannot be reduced to me and my expectations, who cannot be “consumed” or chosen like a product. When love turns into a search for a compatible partner by a list of criteria, it loses its force. Such tenderness is a precious resistance: the capacity to go beyond yourself. Han reminds us that vulnerability in love is not a flaw but its very essence. To love means to let the other remain other.
love.practice: Ask the person you love today about something you don't know about them — a childhood fear, a favorite smell — and take in the answer without checking it against your picture of them.

gratitude.text: Hands in the soil, winter flowers stubbornly opening in January — this is where Han's gratitude comes from. It is a quiet feeling that connects you with the world. In Praise of the Earth Han tells how for several years he tended a garden in Berlin. The garden taught him patience, slowness and wonder at what grows beyond our will. The earth, he writes, is a gift, not a resource; we can relate to it with reverence, not only with calculation. Han might go on: gratitude is the opposite of the logic of achievement. It acknowledges that much in our lives has been received rather than earned. Such a feeling lightens the load: not everything depends on your efforts, and there is relief in that. Gratitude brings you back to the earth, to what is concrete and alive.
gratitude.practice: Touch the soil, the bark of a tree or at least a houseplant, and say to yourself: “I didn't make this.” Keep your palm there for half a minute.

hope.text: The optimist, for Han, risks nothing: he is sure everything will be fine, and needs neither effort nor courage. What you have is different — a more fragile and braver feeling. In The Spirit of Hope Han distinguishes hope from optimism. Hope, by contrast, is born where there is doubt and darkness; it guarantees no outcome, but it opens up the future. Han sets it against fear, which locks a person into the present and the struggle to survive. Hope, as he sees it, is a movement toward what does not yet exist but is possible. This view lets you not be ashamed of your doubts: your hope does not have to be certainty. It can be quiet and unsure — and still remain a force that carries you forward.
hope.practice: Go outside for five minutes and look for signs of what hasn't arrived yet: buds on branches, a house going up, a child learning to walk. Hope, for Han, is a gaze forward, not a forecast.

nostalgia.text: The smell of an old house, the rhythm of Sunday dinner — Han would call this the “scent of time,” something our accelerated time has almost lost. Nostalgia is a warm and slightly bitter feeling, and perhaps its power lies in exactly this loss. In The Scent of Time Han writes that modern time has fallen apart into a string of separate moments, lacking duration and connection. Time used to be filled with rituals, festivals and repetitions that made it habitable. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that in longing for the past, you may be longing not so much for particular events as for a time that had form and rhythm. This insight helps: part of what you remember can be brought back — not as the past itself, but as slowness, a recurring ritual, days that hang together.
nostalgia.practice: Bring one recurring gesture from that time into today — a song, the walk to the bakery, an evening cup of tea — and do it slowly, like a rite.

quote.text: From lack of repose our civilization is turning into a new barbarism.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Human, All Too Human (Han quotes these words in The Burnout Society)

craving.text: Han calls the smartphone a digital object of worship and the like a digital “amen”: the world is built to nudge us every minute. In it, a sharp “I want it now” can be very strong, and needs no shame. In Psychopolitics Han describes a world that works not through prohibitions but through seduction: everything is arranged to stimulate us, reward us and hold on to us. It follows that craving — for the phone, a cigarette, alcohol, anything — often promises a quick release inside a life with no pauses and no point of “enough.” This is neither an excuse nor a verdict, but a way of seeing that you are reaching not only for a substance or a thing, but also for a breather. A wave of desire rises and falls. You can notice it and wait it out without going into battle with it.
craving.practice: When the craving rises, do one thing very slowly — wash a cup, walk across the room, water a plant — and watch how the wave changes over those three minutes.

addiction.text: The achievement-subject, Han writes, dreams of functioning without a stop, and he sees even doping as the logic of the age. If your life has long been organized around something that is hard to get out of, that is hard — and it is not a moral failure. In The Burnout Society Han writes that the modern person has become an “entrepreneur of the self”: they must constantly work on themselves, raise their efficiency, stay in shape. Han would likely note: a substance or a habit sometimes becomes a way to withstand the pressure, or at least to switch off from it for a while. This doesn't make the cycle any less real, but it removes some of the shame. You are not a “bad person” but a person who found a way to cope — and over time that way became too tight. The way out is rarely a heroic leap; more often it is a slow return of pauses, support and people around you.
addiction.practice: Find one pause today that belongs only to you: five minutes by the window, without the phone and without the habit. And if you want to talk with people who know this path from the inside, mutual-help groups are open even for a first quiet visit.

hangover.text: The morning after a party, Han would ask: festival, or mere discharge? A morning of headache, anxiety, memory gaps and shame is hard, and you deserve gentleness, not judgment. Han distinguishes the festival from consumption. The festival, as he sees it, is a time that falls outside the rhythm of work, shared and unhurried. Where there is no festival, all that remains is release: a quick “switching off” before a new cycle of effort. For you this means: the moral hangover is also the voice of the achievement society, which in the morning assesses you as a failed project. But you are not a project. In The Palliative Society Han writes that our culture fears pain and hurries to numb it. A hangover is a time when you can choose not to numb, but to slowly come back to yourself: water, quiet, no conclusions about your personality until evening.
hangover.practice: No conclusions about yourself today. Open a window and stand by it for two minutes, simply breathing and looking out — as a pause, not a punishment.

euphoria.text: To stop time or to speed it up — Han sees a great difference between the two, and it bears on euphoria. A bright high like this can simply be lived and enjoyed. Han would suggest only one distinction: between an uplift and a race. In the achievement society, he writes, “positivity” reigns — everything is possible, everything is available, nothing stops you. Euphoria sometimes resembles a moment when this “everything is possible” is felt from the inside. Han values a different quality of joy — festive, unhurried, connected with the world and with other people, not only with acceleration. Seen through Han's eyes, to keep what is good in this high, you don't have to turn it immediately into plans, decisions and achievements. You can let it be, like a festival that serves no purpose. Then it will leave behind not only traces of effort but also a memory of lightness.
euphoria.practice: Stand still for a minute inside this high and feel how your heart beats and how you breathe. Put big decisions off until tomorrow — a festival decides nothing.

crash.text: In old villages, ordinary days followed the festival, and no one was frightened: time had a rhythm. Han would likely see your drop after a high as the same change of rhythm — heavy, fall-like, yet natural. Han writes that the typical illnesses of our time are not “infections” but rather “infarctions”: not a blow from outside, but exhaustion from excess — of stimuli, of effort, of positivity. Translated into the language of your life, the comedown is not proof that something is wrong with you but the natural flip side of the high. Han defends the right to negativity — to moments when you are not at your peak, not productive and not shining. The slump doesn't have to be fixed. It can be lived as a time of quiet, when strength returns slowly, without the demand to get back in shape right away.
crash.practice: Choose one very small task for today — water a plant, make the bed — and do it slowly, like a ritual. The rest can wait: a comedown needs time, not a sprint.

panic.text: “Every age has its signature afflictions” — so Han begins The Burnout Society, and our age, as he sees it, is marked by the exhaustion of the nervous system from excess, overload, constant stimulation. When panic hits — your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something irreparable is happening — it is very hard, and you are not alone in it. Han might put it this way: a wave of panic is not only your personal breakdown but also the body's response to a world with few pauses. Right now, in the middle of the wave, philosophy is not the main thing. The main thing is that such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don't have to fight it; you can lean on what is slow and reliable: the floor, your breath, the things around you.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and find support in things: touch the table, the wall, some fabric, and slowly name each one aloud. Make each out-breath longer than the in-breath — heavy, unhurried things will help you wait until the wave begins to ebb.

dread.text: The question “what is it all for?” our culture tries to drown out like noise behind a wall, and Han considers this one of its main mistakes. The sense of the abyss and of finitude is one of the deepest human experiences, and it does not make you weaker. In The Palliative Society Han writes that we fear all negativity and strive for a state with neither pain nor mystery — only endless survival and optimization. When meaning is reduced to efficiency, the question “what for?” inevitably rises from within. Taking Han's thought further, your dread is also a longing for something greater than you, for what cannot be measured by usefulness. Han sees the answer not in quick consolation but in contemplation and connection — with the earth, with another person, with slow time in which life regains its weight.
dread.practice: Go out for five minutes to a place where something living grows, and stand beside a tree or some grass without asking anything. Han would say: it too is finite — and it grows all the same.

fomo.text: The feed is endless; you are not. For Han, that mismatch breeds the feeling that everyone else lives more interesting lives and you're in the wrong place. It is common, and it has a source. In the achievement society life itself becomes a project to be optimized, and digital networks turn it into a shop window. Han calls this the “hell of the same”: we see endless variations of the same successful pictures, and each of them says “you could have had more.” Han would probably say: the fear of missing out is the voice of the endless “you can,” which never says “enough.” But life, for Han, gains depth not from the number of possibilities but from attention to what is already near. The fact that you are not everywhere is not a loss; it is the condition for truly being somewhere.
fomo.practice: Leave your phone at home and walk for five minutes, collecting three impressions that can't be posted: a smell, a sound, the temperature of the air.

sleepless.text: A door, an evening prayer, a shop shut for the night — Han values thresholds that told time “it ends here.” Three a.m. thoughts are exhausting, and you needn't blame yourself for them. In The Scent of Time Han writes about the crisis of modern time: it falls apart into a string of moments with no rhythm and no closure. There are no longer thresholds separating work from rest, day from night — everything is open, everything is available, everything goes on. The simple conclusion: night thoughts are the day's unfinished business that found no place of its own. Sleep, in the thought of Walter Benjamin, on whom Han draws, is the high point of bodily rest, and it cannot be seized by effort. You can only prepare a place for it: not solving the day's tasks at night, and letting your thoughts wait until morning.
sleepless.practice: Make a small threshold for the night: put your phone face down in a far corner of the room, say aloud “that's all for today,” and breathe out slowly three times.

betrayal.text: We always trust a little blindly, and Han sees this not as a flaw but as the condition of closeness. So betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only the bond but your faith in your own ability to trust. In The Transparency Society Han says something subtle about trust: it is only possible between knowing and not knowing. If we knew everything about another person, trust would be unnecessary; we trust precisely because we cannot check everything. Han might add: your trust was not naivety or a mistake. It was a brave step toward an Other who always remains not fully transparent. Betrayal shows how fragile that step is, but it doesn't make it meaningless. Han warns against the temptation of total control. Instead of never opening up to anyone again, you can give yourself time — and acknowledge that the capacity to trust remains your strength.
betrayal.practice: Walk for five minutes and silently list the people you still trust in small things: a neighbor, the bus driver, a friend. Trust has not vanished — it has been wounded.

jealousy.text: Socrates was called atopos, “placeless”: he could be neither figured out nor possessed. Han believes a loved one stays like this too — which is why jealousy, a tormenting and deeply human feeling, hurts so. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that love is an encounter with the “atopic” Other: a person who can never be fully put in their place, understood and possessed. This is both the mystery and the risk of love. Here is what follows: jealousy arises when the otherness of the person you love is felt as a threat — they live their own life, which you cannot fully know or hold on to. That hurts. But Han would warn: the attempt to make the Other fully transparent and your own destroys eros itself. Your jealousy speaks of how much this person means to you. You can acknowledge this fear without turning it into control.
jealousy.practice: Imagine you knew absolutely everything about the person you love — every thought, every minute. Stay inside that picture for a minute and ask yourself: would anything be left in them to love?

resentment.text: Han did not write about resentment as such, but The Scent of Time has an image that fits it: time that neither flows nor comes to a close, but gets stuck. An old grudge is a weight you carry around, and it often preserves the memory of a real injustice. A grudge is like a stuck moment: the event is long past but has found no closure. Han values rituals as forms that allow us to close chapters of life. Letting go of a grudge does not mean saying that nothing happened, nor does it necessarily mean forgiving. It means gradually letting what happened take its place in the past, and letting yourself return to the present, where you are more than this wound.
resentment.practice: Perform a small closing ritual: squeeze a pebble or a crumpled scrap of paper in your fist, name the grudge silently, and put the object on a shelf. A chapter can be closed without pretending it never happened.

heartbreak.text: A door torn off by the wind won't shut as before — roughly how Han sees real love: it knocks us out of ourselves. So a broken heart truly hurts, and this pain needn't be rushed. In The Agony of Eros Han defends what he calls the negativity of love. In his view, contemporary culture wants love without risk or vulnerability — “comfortable,” predictable, like a favorable exchange. But real eros, Han writes, is an encounter with the Other that can wound and change us, rather than confirm what we already knew about ourselves. In other words, your pain is not a sign of failure but evidence that you truly met another person and opened up to them. Han would suggest not “optimizing” grief and not hurrying to turn the page, but giving it time: such a wound is part of the capacity to love.
heartbreak.practice: Put on one song that is exactly about what you feel and listen to the end, sitting still, with no phone in your hands. Let the sadness last exactly one song.

impostor.text: A staircase with no top step — that is one way to picture life in the achievement society as Han sees it. No wonder so many conscientious people fear they are about to be exposed. In the achievement society, he writes, a person is both their own worker and their own overseer: the evaluation never ends, and the bar rises with every success. In The Transparency Society he describes a culture of constant exposure, where everything must be visible and measurable. Han might go on: impostor feelings are not proof that you are “not the real thing” but a natural response to a world where no one can ever be “good enough.” If the bar will rise again tomorrow anyway, then today's anxiety says more about the system than about you. You can allow yourself to be a learner rather than flawless.
impostor.practice: Say aloud three things you really can do — dryly, as facts, without “just” or “only.” Han would say: this is a step you can stand on.

self_hatred.text: Exploiter and exploited in one person — this is how Han describes the person of our century, at war with themselves. If your inner voice is merciless toward you, that is very hard, and it does not tell the truth about you. Han describes its origin like this: in the achievement society there is no external master, so a person begins to exploit themselves. They become at once the one who demands and the one from whom it is demanded — and wage war on themselves. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that a harsh inner critic is in large part the internalized voice of an era that is never satisfied. Its verdicts sound like your own, but they are not entirely yours. Han looks for a way out not in even more effort against yourself, but in friendliness, pause and attention to the world around you.
self_hatred.practice: When the critic speaks, say its sentence out loud — and then immediately retell it in the voice you use with a close friend. Listen to the difference.

helplessness.text: “I can do anything” and “nothing depends on me” are, for Han, two sides of one coin. Helplessness is heavy, especially when it seems you decide nothing, and it deserves compassion. In Psychopolitics Han notices a paradox: in the achievement society a person considers themselves completely free, so they attribute any failure to themselves alone. Instead of seeing the shared conditions, they turn their discontent against themselves — and instead of protest comes exhaustion. It follows that your powerlessness may partly be an honest knowledge that much really is out of your hands. That is not your fault. Han also defends another kind of strength — the ability to say “no,” to stop, to not take part in the endless race. Sometimes the first step out of helplessness is not a leap but a refusal to demand the impossible of yourself.
helplessness.practice: Do one thing today that is surely in your hands and takes two minutes: move a chair, take out the trash, answer one message. And allow yourself to demand nothing more.

procrastination.text: Bartleby, the scrivener in Melville's story, answered every request with “I would prefer not to” — and Han devotes pages of The Burnout Society to him. A stuck “I can't get started” is neither laziness nor a character defect. In the achievement society, he writes, every task becomes an exam: it must be done well, fast, better than before. When every task is a test of your worth, starting is frightening. Han also speaks of “hyperactivity” and multitasking: attention is scattered among dozens of stimuli, and deep concentration becomes ever harder. Han would likely note: procrastination can be an overloaded person's protest against the endless “you can.” Han values the ability not to do — as a pause, not as a defeat. Once you allow yourself rest without guilt, it is often easier to take the first small step.
procrastination.practice: Make only the very first move — open the file, put the notebook on the table — and stop. Stand over it for a minute, as at a threshold, demanding nothing of yourself.

uprooted.text: Han left Seoul for Germany as a very young man, and the ground under one's feet is no abstraction for him. When home, language and familiar streets are left behind, it affects a person deeply, and your sense of loss is legitimate. In The Disappearance of Rituals Han describes rituals as what makes time habitable, the way a house makes space habitable. In Praise of the Earth he tells of his garden in Berlin: of how tending the soil, the plants and the turning seasons brings back a sense of rootedness. For you this means: home is not only a place on a map but also recurring gestures, rhythms, familiar things. These can gradually be created anew. Not replacing what was lost, but growing new soil beside it — slowly, the way a garden grows.
uprooted.practice: Choose one fixed point — a window, a bench, a tree along your way — and starting today, greet it every day, even if only with a glance. This is how new ground grows: slowly, like a garden.

overload.text: A scroll, a notification, one more tab — Han would say this is how attention shatters into a thousand pieces. Overload from such a stream is real fatigue, not your inability to “cope.” In In the Swarm Han mentions “information fatigue syndrome”: an excess of information doesn't make us smarter but dulls our ability to judge and to discern. He distinguishes hyperattention — rapid switching between stimuli — from deep attention, which is necessary for contemplation and thought. Seen through Han's eyes, your overload is a natural response to a world where the stream never ends. Han proposes not to “manage” the stream better, but sometimes to step out of it. Attention is not an infinite resource, and letting it rest is care, not escape.
overload.practice: Turn off everything that can beep or light up for five minutes and sit in silence with your eyes closed. Han would call this the return of deep attention — even if only for a little while.

unreality.text: Han keeps a jukebox at home, heavy as a small wardrobe, and in Non-things he praises it for a simple virtue: it can be touched. When the world around you, or you yourself, seems unreal, that is unsettling and strange, and it deserves gentle treatment. In the same book he writes about how information displaces things: we touch the dense, weighty world less and less and live more and more among streams of data, screens and images. The world becomes smooth and intangible. Translated into the language of your life, the experience of unreality resonates with an era in which reality is already losing its weight. This doesn't explain everything, but it can make the feeling less frightening. Han looks for support in things that resist: in soil, in weight, in texture, in slow touch. Sometimes the way back leads through simple sensations of the body and of things.
unreality.practice: Pick up the heaviest object nearby — a book, a stone, a mug — and for a minute feel its weight, temperature, roughness. A thing, for Han, gives the world back its density.

awe.text: Jeff Koons's gleaming sculptures, without a single rough spot, are Han's example of a beauty that asks nothing of us. Real awe before something vast or beautiful works differently, and this rare experience is worth living to the full. In Saving Beauty Han distinguishes the smooth from the beautiful. The smooth is what pleases instantly, offers no resistance and demands nothing, like a polished screen. The beautiful, for Han, carries something of a wound: it shakes you, stops you, takes you beyond your usual “I.” Han might put it this way: your awe is a moment when the world stops being mere background for your affairs and becomes something greater. It holds the very negativity Han defends — an encounter with what does not belong to you. Such an experience doesn't need to be photographed or explained right away. It is enough to let it hold you still.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what moved you, without taking out your phone. If it is the sky, the sea or trees, try breathing in time with what you see.

relief.text: An out-breath that doesn't have to be followed at once by a gulp of air for the next push — Han values this above many achievements. Something heavy has let go, and this is a warm, well-earned feeling. Han would suggest seeing a special value in relief — as in a pause. He writes about the Sabbath as a day that exists not to restore strength before new work, but for its own sake: a time in which nothing needs to be produced. In the achievement society relief often turns at once into “now I can get on with the next thing.” Taking Han's thought further, don't hurry to convert relief into new tasks. This moment is not an empty space between two efforts but a small piece of the good life in itself. You can let it last, like a festival that serves no purpose.
relief.practice: Take three slow out-breaths, each longer than the in-breath, and on the last one say to yourself: “Nothing is needed right now.” The next task can wait one more minute.

calm.text: In a Japanese rock garden there is nothing to do — you can only look; Han, who has written on Zen Buddhism, values exactly such places. Your calm is a precious state, and in it you can simply be. Han defends the vita contemplativa — the contemplative life — setting it against endless activity. In The Burnout Society he recalls Nietzsche's idea of a “pedagogy of seeing”: learning to see means accustoming the eye to calm and patience, letting things come close to us. Han would probably say: your calm is not idleness or lost time but the return of deep attention, in which the world becomes visible again. It doesn't need to be used for anything. Han would say that it is precisely in such moments that a person stops being a project and becomes simply alive.
calm.practice: Choose one object in the room and look at it for a minute as if it were a stone in a Japanese garden: without judging, without adding thoughts, simply letting it be.

quote.text: Learning to see — accustoming the eye to calmness, to patience, to letting things come up to it.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Twilight of the Idols (Han quotes these words in The Burnout Society)

inspiration.text: Ideas, for Han, come not to those who run but to those who linger. Inspiration is a joyful and lively feeling, and you can meet it with gratitude. In The Burnout Society Han writes that creativity is born of deep attention and even of deep boredom — of a state in which we are not busy with endless switching. Drawing on Benjamin, Han says that without such calm the “dream bird” that hatches experience flies away. The simple conclusion: inspiration is not a result of pressure and self-optimization but a gift of slow, open time. It doesn't have to be turned into a product right away. You can let it live, play, and let the idea unfold while it is not yet obliged to be useful.
inspiration.practice: Before you turn the idea into a plan, take it for a slow five-minute walk. Let it play a little longer before it has to become useful.

schadenfreude.text: When everyone becomes an “entrepreneur of the self,” life turns into a nonstop competition, and someone else's success feels like your own loss — this is how Han describes the achievement society. Schadenfreude is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but it grows out of exactly this race. In such a world another person's failure eases the pressure for a moment: “it's not only me who can't manage.” Han might add: schadenfreude is less a character trait than a symptom of fatigue from endless comparison. Han writes that comparison makes everyone the same and deprives us of a genuine encounter with the Other — a person who is not a rival but simply different. When you notice schadenfreude, you don't have to punish yourself; you can ask where you yourself have grown tired of the race.
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine for a minute that no rankings exist — no salaries, no likes, no grades. Who would this person be to you then — a rival, or simply someone else?

contempt.text: How many seconds did you look at this person before deciding they weren't worth your attention? That is exactly what Han would ask. In In the Swarm Han reflects on respect and reminds us that the German Respekt goes back to the Latin respicere — “to look back, to look closely.” Respect, for Han, requires distance: the ability to look at another person without merging with them or appropriating them. The digital environment, he believes, destroys this distance: everything becomes instant, close and public, and instead of respect come waves of disregard. Here is what follows: contempt is often born of too quick a glance. You are not obliged to respect someone who has caused harm. But you can give yourself time to look more closely — and then contempt will either give way to understanding or become a calm, clear boundary.
contempt.practice: Look at this person “a second time,” as the word respicere asks: recall one trait or act of theirs that doesn't fit your verdict. Just one is enough.

disgust.text: Han sees the smartphone's smooth screen as the emblem of the age: pleasant to touch, demanding nothing. Disgust is a strong, bodily feeling that often has its reasons, but sometimes it grows from this love of the smooth. In Saving Beauty Han writes that contemporary culture gravitates toward “the smooth”: flawless surfaces, filtered photos, everything that doesn't scratch or resist. Negativity is pushed out of the world — everything uneven, imperfect, truly bodily. In other words, the smoother our familiar world becomes, the more easily disgust flares up at anything that breaks that smoothness. This doesn't mean your disgust is wrong: sometimes it honestly warns of a boundary that has been crossed. But if it is aimed at yourself or at human imperfection, Han would remind you: what is alive is never smooth. Roughness is a sign of reality, not a flaw.
disgust.practice: Touch something rough and imperfect — bark, old fabric, your own palm — and for a minute simply feel the unevenness. Then ask: is my disgust warning me of danger, or simply of something alive?

revenge.text: A fist clenched in a pocket hits no one — except the one clenching it. Han would likely describe a revenge that can't be acted on this way: a natural response to injustice that easily turns against you. In Topology of Violence Han traces how violence changes its form over time: from open clashes to hidden, inner pressure that a person turns against themselves. Han might go on: a wish for revenge that cannot and need not be acted on easily turns into endlessly replaying the hurt — that is, into quiet violence against yourself. Han values the contemplative pause — the ability not to respond instantly. Your feeling deserves attention, not execution and not suppression. Beneath it there is often a thirst for recognition: for the pain done to you to be seen. This need can be respected without harming either the other person or yourself.
revenge.practice: Unclench your fists, rest your palms on your knees and take five slow out-breaths. Then think about whom you could tell exactly how you were hurt — recognition is often needed more than revenge.

anger_at_loved.text: Two people sit silently in a kitchen, each in their own tiredness, and any word could spark — a scene straight out of Handke's Essay on Tiredness. Anger at those close to us often comes when strength runs out, and shame follows. In The Burnout Society Han, drawing on Handke, distinguishes two kinds of tiredness. One is separating: it makes people mute and irritable, locks each person inside themselves, and loved ones suddenly start to seem like an obstacle. The other is a tiredness that trusts the world and brings people closer, as after doing something together. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that anger at loved ones often speaks not of a lack of love but of the exhaustion of someone who has spent all day squeezing results out of themselves. Don't take it out on those around you, but don't punish yourself either. Notice instead: you need rest, not one more effort.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises, say one sentence to them out loud: “I'm very tired right now, give me ten minutes.” And spend those minutes in silence, in another room.

ambivalence.text: “I wish they were different” and “I love them as they are” — Han would not choose between these two sentences. Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is hard, but deeply human. In The Agony of Eros Han criticizes the idea of love as something comfortable and “positive,” free of risk and pain. Such love, he writes, turns into consumption: we want only what is pleasant and convenient from the other. But the real Other, for Han, is always unlike us and resists our expectations — that is their “negativity.” It follows that your ambivalence is a sign that there is a real person beside you, not a convenient reflection. Irritation and tenderness intertwine because the Other does not submit to you. You don't have to choose one of the feelings: both speak of a living, complicated bond.
ambivalence.practice: Say both sentences to yourself in a row, about one and the same trait: “It annoys me that you…” and “I love that you…”. Notice whether it is one and the same otherness.

guilty_relief.text: Someone who has finally set down heavy bags needn't explain why they feel lighter — Han would likely start there. After a breakup, a job ended, or a loved one's long illness, relief can arrive with guilt: how can I feel this? Han writes that the modern person has forgotten how to stop: they live in a mode of endless “more,” where a breather feels like weakness. Caring for someone who is ill, a difficult relationship, an exhausting job all demand strength that is not infinite. Han reminds us of the Sabbath — a day when people stop working not in order to recover for new work but for the sake of rest itself. Han would likely note: relief is your body and soul finally receiving the right to pause. It does not cancel the love and care you have given. You can allow yourself this exhale without judging yourself.
guilty_relief.practice: Set down imaginary bags: drop your shoulders, open your hands, breathe out. Stay like this for a minute — relief does not cancel the love you carried.

indifference.text: A painting in a museum that people pass in three seconds moves no one — and Han would ask what the painting has to do with it. When something that “should” move you leaves you cold, it's easy to get scared for yourself. Han describes an era of excess: an endless stream of information, images, news. In The Burnout Society he speaks of “hyperattention” — a scattered switching among many stimuli in which it is impossible to linger on anything. But a feeling needs time: without it, an impression just slides across the surface. For you this means: your indifference is not necessarily callousness; it may be overload, in which the soul simply stops responding. Han defends deep, contemplative attention — slow and focused. Feeling can come back if you give it silence and time, rather than demanding an immediate “right” reaction from yourself.
indifference.practice: Choose one thing that “should” move you and look at it for five minutes without distraction, like a painting in an empty museum. Demand nothing — just let time do its work.

escape.text: What exactly do you want to run from — the city, or whoever keeps driving you on? Han would ask this first. The wish to drop everything often appears when life has turned into one long obligation. Han describes the “achievement-subject,” who believes they are free but in fact exploits themselves: “you can” becomes a compulsion stronger than any order. No wonder you want to leave — although the inner overseer is easy to take along to any city. Seen through Han's eyes, the wish to escape is the voice of the part of you that wants not new productivity but rest, idleness, time that belongs to no one. Han calls this the contemplative life, the vita contemplativa. You don't have to change everything at once. You can start with a small “escape” into unhurriedness — and hear what you really want.
escape.practice: Take a five-minute “escape” without your phone: step out into the yard or the stairwell and walk slowly, going nowhere. Listen to what the part of you that asks to leave really wants.

forbidden_attraction.text: A spark jumps where different charges meet, not identical ones — Han would likely explain any strong attraction so. Being drawn to someone unavailable, or “the wrong person,” can be unsettling. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that genuine eros is directed at the Other in their otherness — at someone who cannot be possessed, explained or fitted into our schemes. He uses the Greek word atopos — “having no place,” elusive; this is what Socrates' interlocutors called him. Eros, for Han, flares up precisely before the atopic — before what breaks out of the familiar order. Translated into the language of your life, your attraction speaks not of some corruption in you but of a longing to meet something truly other in a world where everything has become the same and available. It needs neither to be condemned nor to be rushed. You can ask with curiosity: what otherness have I encountered in this person?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Try a thought experiment: imagine this attraction not as a person but as a direction. Toward what otherness, what world is it calling you? Sometimes you can step into that world without this person.

social_anxiety.text: A jury in every phone — that is one way to describe the world of The Transparency Society, where, for Han, every gesture is tested for “likes.” Fearing people and their judgment is hard in such a world: any gathering becomes an ordeal. No wonder many people feel as if they are on stage and afraid of making a mistake. Han might put it this way: part of your anxiety is a response to a culture of constant exposure, not only a personal trait. Han defends the right to opacity, to silence, to not being fully visible. In this light, shyness is not a flaw but a way of taking care of your own inner life. You are not obliged to perform or make an impression. You can simply be present, listen, and allow yourself to stay a little closed.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a gathering, press your feet into the floor, feel the back of the chair and tell yourself: “I'm not performing, I'm just here.” At the gathering itself, choose the role of listener — that too is presence.

uncertainty.text: A weather forecast soothes, but it doesn't teach hope — Han would likely start from this distinction. When nothing is guaranteed it is exhausting, and you crave some certainty. In The Spirit of Hope Han distinguishes hope from optimism. Optimism is sure in advance that everything will be fine — it has nothing to overcome. Hope, by contrast, is born where the future is open and guaranteed by nothing: it knows failure is possible and yet turns toward what does not yet exist. Han sets it against fear, which shuts a person up inside themselves. Taking Han's thought further, uncertainty is not only a source of anxiety but also the very space in which hope is possible at all. If everything were known in advance, there would be nothing to hope for. Instead of trying to guess the future, you can ask yourself: what, in spite of everything, do I hope for?
uncertainty.practice: Go to the window and look at the sky: it makes no promises about tomorrow's weather. Say quietly: “I don't know what will happen, but I hope that…” — and finish the sentence without checking whether it is realistic.

waiting.text: Water in a kettle boils at its own pace, however you watch it. Han would likely say that waiting — for an answer, results, news — wears us out because we've forgotten how to live at such a pace. In The Scent of Time Han writes that modern time has fallen apart into a string of points: we hurry from one event to the next, and everything in between seems empty and lost. Hence the torment of waiting — it drops out of the chain of “useful” moments. Han proposes giving time back its “scent”: learning to linger, to dwell in duration and not only in the result. Han would probably say: waiting is not necessarily a hole in life. It is also time that can be lived — slowly, with attention to what is near. The answer will come when it comes, and this hour is already yours.
waiting.practice: While you wait, make a cup of tea and follow the whole process — the sound of the water, the steam, the color in the cup — as slowly as if it were your only task today.

regret.text: A list of failures and the story of a life are, for Han, two entirely different ways of remembering. Regret over what you did or didn't do pulls you back into the past again and again. In The Crisis of Narration Han writes that today we live among information — scattered facts that quickly go out of date — and are losing the ability to tell stories. Yet it is narrative that ties events into meaning: in a story the past doesn't disappear but becomes part of a path. The simple conclusion: regret is especially painful as long as the mistake remains an isolated fact, an item on an imaginary list of failures. When you write it into the story of your life — with what came before and what came after — it finds its place. A past that has been told stops being a verdict and becomes a chapter.
regret.practice: Write three sentences about that choice: what came before, what happened, what came after. Read them aloud — as a chapter, not a verdict.

longing.text: A message, a photo, a call — today everything is within reach in a second, and so, for Han, we have forgotten how to bear absence. To miss a particular person is to feel the presence of their absence. Han writes that eros is always bound up with distance: the Other is never fully accessible, and it is precisely this unreachability that makes them a living person rather than an object. Han might add: your longing is not a malfunction but a form of faithfulness to a specific, irreplaceable person. It cannot be filled with a substitute: in the “hell of the same” that Han criticizes, everything is interchangeable, but the person you love is not. You don't have to drive the longing away; you can carry it gently within you as a sign that this person is the only one of their kind for you.
longing.practice: Recall one detail of this person — a voice, a gesture, a habit — and hold it in memory for a minute, slowly, the way you hold an old object in your hands, without opening your phone.

world_pain.text: Han distinguishes two ways of failing to bear others' pain: turning away from it, or drowning in its endless stream. News of war, injustice and suffering arrives without pause, and the pain for the world can be immense. In The Palliative Society Han describes “algophobia” — a fear of pain that makes contemporary culture try to anesthetize everything and avoid seeing suffering. Against this background your pain is a sign that you have not turned away and that others' suffering touches you. For Han, this is exactly the openness to the Other that is so lacking in a society where everything must be pleasant. But Han also warns about the stream of information that pours down without respite and leaves no room to make sense of anything. In this light you are not obliged to let the whole stream in. Less news and more silence help your pain remain a human response rather than a stunned numbness.
world_pain.practice: Choose one time of day for the news, and after it — three minutes of silence: sit with your palms on your knees and let what you've read settle.

rejection.text: A swipe left takes half a second, and Han sees a whole philosophy of our time in it. Rejection feels like being judged whole and found unfit. Han describes a “society of positivity” in which relationships increasingly resemble a market: we scroll, rate, “like” and turn people down with a flick of a finger. In this logic a refusal feels like a verdict on your “market value.” Here is what follows: this is the logic of consumption, not the truth about a person. He writes that a real encounter with the Other is impossible in the mode of choosing a product — it needs time, openness and risk. In this light, rejection is not a verdict on your worth but a sign that the encounter didn't happen. The pain of it is honest and deserves attention. But you are not a profile that failed to make the cut.
rejection.practice: Call someone who has known you for a long time and talk for five minutes about anything at all. You are not a profile, and a living voice will remind you of that.

abandonment.text: A bridge rests not on one pillar but on many — Han would probably say the same about a human life. The fear of being abandoned runs very deep: it feels as if your support could vanish at any moment. In The Disappearance of Rituals Han writes that rituals — repeated shared actions — make time habitable, like a home: they give stability and a sense that the world goes on. Today, for Han, there are fewer and fewer rituals; relationships become fluid and noncommittal, and a person has nothing to lean on but their own efforts. In other words, your fear partly reflects a general lack of stability, not only your personal vulnerability. You can also look for support in small rituals — regular meetings, shared habits, days that belong to you and the people close to you.
abandonment.practice: Suggest a small recurring ritual to someone close today — a Sunday call, tea together on Thursdays. A small support, repeated many times, holds firm.

unrequited.text: An outstretched hand that no one took is still an outstretched hand — Han would probably say this of love without an answer. The feeling is there, but there is no answer, and it hurts. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that love in its essence is an encounter with an Other who cannot be possessed or disposed of. Contemporary culture, as he sees it, wants love without risk — like a purchase that is guaranteed to pay off. But genuine eros always includes the possibility of getting no answer; that is its “negativity” and its seriousness. Han might go on: your love, even unrequited, is evidence that you are capable of going beyond yourself toward the Other — and that, for Han, happens less and less in an age of widespread narcissism. The pain does not devalue the feeling. It was a real movement toward someone.
unrequited.practice: Stretch out your hand in front of you, palm up, and hold it there for half a minute, breathing slowly. It is the gesture of someone able to reach out — and it stays yours, even without an answer.

humiliation.text: The crowd's laughter dies down in a minute, but a person stays alone with that minute for a long time. Humiliation, especially in front of others, feels like losing the ground under your feet, and Han writes about its digital form — the shitstorms of In the Swarm. He notes that there is no respect in them, no distance, no time for understanding. A similar logic works on a smaller scale too: mockery, public judgment, being put on display. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that humiliation often says more about a culture of instant exposure, and about those who humiliate, than about you. Han defends the right to opacity — to an inner space that no one else's gaze can reach. There you remain yourself, however loud the outside noise.
humiliation.practice: Close the door, draw the curtains and sit for two minutes where no one's gaze can reach. Tell yourself: “No one is judging me here.”

body_shame.text: A filter that erases wrinkles in a fraction of a second Han would call a small monument to the age of the smooth. Being unhappy with your body has cultural roots. In Saving Beauty Han writes that our era worships “the smooth”: polished surfaces, filters, flawless images. In such a culture the body turns into a shop window that must be constantly polished and put on display, and we keep looking at ourselves through the eyes of an imagined viewer, as in an endless selfie. It follows that your dissatisfaction is largely produced by this gaze, not by an objective truth about you. A living body is never smooth: it has marks, asymmetry, a history. Han believes that beauty is connected precisely with depth and unevenness, not with a flawless surface.
body_shame.practice: Run your fingers over one “trace of history” on your body — a scar, a mole, a callus — and recall what stretch of life it holds. The smooth remembers nothing, but you do.

illness.text: A hospital room is one of the few places where time still flows slowly, and Han would probably see in this more than just misfortune. When your body lets you down, fear, fatigue and sometimes anger come — and all of it is human. In The Palliative Society Han writes that contemporary culture strives to push pain and illness out of sight: suffering seems a meaningless obstacle to be removed as quickly as possible. So a person who is ill often feels guilty on top of everything, as if they had become “inefficient.” Han argues against this: pain, as he sees it, is part of human experience, not simply a glitch in a mechanism. Han would likely note: you are not obliged to stay productive and “positive” while ill. You can allow yourself to slow down and accept care from others — this is not weakness but honesty toward your own body.
illness.practice: Place your hand on the part of you that hurts or is tired and whisper to it: “Today I'm not rushing you anywhere.” Breathe like this for a minute.

pride.text: “Done” is a rare word in the achievement society: Han notes that its subject never reaches the point where it can be said. That is why pride in what you have done, healthy and well-deserved, struggles to appear here. Every success instantly becomes a step toward the next one, and satisfaction slips away. It is precisely this perpetual unfinishedness, for Han, that feeds burnout. For you this means: healthy pride is a small ritual of completion, a moment when you allow a task to end. Don't rush straight to the next task. Stop, look at what has been done, and let it stand for a while. This is not vanity but an important pause, one our time lacks so badly.
pride.practice: Rest your hand on what you have made — a folder, a tool, a screen with the finished file — and stand with it for a minute in silence, as before a completed building.

melancholy.text: A huge blue planet slowly approaches the Earth — Han opens The Agony of Eros with this image from Lars von Trier's Melancholia. Gentle sadness, like that film, is a quiet feeling that holds depth. Han reads the heroine's depression as a closing-in on the self, and the approaching planet as an image of the wholly Other that tears a person out of that enclosure. Seen through Han's eyes, melancholy can cut both ways. It can lock you inside yourself — or, on the contrary, make you sensitive to what lies beyond everyday bustle: fragility, beauty, time slipping away. This gentle sadness is close to the contemplation Han values so highly. It doesn't need to be “fixed” — it can be lived unhurriedly, like an evening with nothing to do.
melancholy.practice: Go for a five-minute evening walk and move more slowly than usual, letting the sadness walk beside you. Don't intensify it and don't chase it away.
